title: Pressure-cooker beef brisket
subtitle: Sliceable, fork-tender brisket in 90 minutes
excerpt: Beef brisket braised under pressure in a spiced, savoury liquid until it yields into clean slices. A cut that usually requires half a day of low-and-slow cooking delivered in under two hours.
sourceNotes: Beef brisket is a working muscle that requires long, moist cooking to break down its collagen, traditionally achieved by smoking (Texas-style), pot-roasting (Jewish brisket), or braising (British). The pressure-cooker version compresses the 4 to 6 hour oven braise into 90 minutes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely and slice before freezing. Freeze in containers with sauce for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Brisket is better the following day. Cook, cool, refrigerate in the sauce overnight, then slice and reheat gently.

content.text: Beef brisket is a long-muscle cut from the chest, richly flavoured but tough without extended cooking. The pressure cooker breaks down its collagen in 90 minutes where the oven would take five or six hours. The result is brisket that slices cleanly, holds its shape on the plate, and melts under a fork.

Sear the brisket well on all sides before sealing the lid. This is a non-negotiable step, the Maillard browning from a hot pan gives the finished dish its depth of colour and flavour. The braising liquid cannot add browning; it can only carry what you build first.

Slicing across the grain is equally important. Brisket has long, visible muscle fibres, cutting with the grain produces chewy strands; cutting against it produces short, tender pieces. Look at the meat before you slice.

items.prepNote: tied with string if needed to keep shape

content.text: Pat the brisket dry and season generously with salt and pepper on all sides. Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large frying pan over high heat until just smoking. Sear the brisket for 4 to 5 minutes per side until deeply browned. Transfer to the pressure cooker.

Reduce the heat in the frying pan to medium. Add the onion and carrot; cook for 5 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato puree; stir for 1 minute. Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping the base of the pan. Pour over the brisket in the pressure cooker. Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock, the thyme, and the bay.

Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 90 minutes. Allow a full natural pressure release, at least 20 minutes. Do not quick-release. Open the lid and test: the meat should be tender and a skewer should slide through with very little resistance.

Lift the brisket out carefully and rest on a board for 20 minutes. Strain the braising liquid and reduce in a saucepan over high heat for 8 minutes until it coats the back of a spoon. Slice the brisket against the grain into 1 cm slices. Serve with the sauce.

rows.symptom: The brisket is tough after 90 minutes
rows.cause: The joint was particularly large or dense, or the cooker did not reach full pressure throughout.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 20 to 30 minutes. Brisket is very hard to overcook in a pressure cooker, additional time only adds tenderness.

rows.symptom: The slices fall apart on cutting
rows.cause: The brisket was overcooked, or did not rest long enough before slicing.
rows.fix: If the brisket is too tender to slice, serve it pulled with a fork rather than sliced. This is not a failure, it is delicious.

rows.cause: The braising liquid was not reduced after cooking.
rows.fix: Strain the liquid and boil rapidly in a wide saucepan for 10 to 15 minutes until it reduces to a sauce consistency.

content.text: Brisket is one of the best make-ahead dishes there is. Cook it the day before, cool in the braising liquid, and refrigerate overnight. The next day, slice the cold meat (it holds together much better cold than hot), arrange in a baking dish, pour the reheated sauce over, cover with foil, and warm in a low oven for 20 minutes. The flavour is noticeably better than on the day of cooking.

Brisket suits a Sunday table or a dinner for guests, it is a communal cut that serves six without fuss once it is on the board. The pressure cooker version removes the main barrier, which is time, and makes it accessible as a weekday meal for households that can spare 90 minutes of unattended cooking. Serve with mashed potato, roast vegetables, or simply with good bread and the sauce.
